manual_retrieved_paragraphs.text: Here we show that iron is a key driver of nodulation because symbiotic nodules cannot form without iron, even under conditions of sufficient light and low nitrogen. We further identify an iron optimum for soybean nodulation and the iron sensor BRUTUS A (BTSa) which acts as a hub for integrating iron and nodulation cues. BTSa is induced by rhizobia, binds to and is stabilized by iron. In turn, BTSa stabilizes and enhances the transcriptional activation activity of pro-nodulation transcription factor NSP1a by monoubiquitination from its RING domain and consequently activates nodulation signalling. Monoubiquitination of NSP1 by BTS is conserved in legumes to trigger nodulation under iron sufficiency. Thus, iron status is an essential cue to trigger nodulation and BTSa integrates cues from rhizobial infection and iron status to orchestrate host responses towards establishing symbiotic nitrogen fixation.

manual_retrieved_paragraphs.text: To determine the role of iron in soybean nodulation, we initially investigated its effect on nodulation. We inoculated the soybean reference cultivar Williams 82 (Wm82) with Bradyrhizobium diazoefficiens USDA110 rhizobia in a hydroponic growth setup with iron (Fe–EDTA) concentrations of 0, 0.4, 40 and 400 μM under low-nitrogen and sufficient light conditions. Plants formed the highest number of nodules at 40 μM iron, and almost no nodules at 0 and 400 μM iron. Consistently, infection number and primordia number were dramatically decreased under 0 and 400 μM iron (Extended Data Fig. 1a–f). To ascertain the optimal iron concentration for nodulation, we then conducted a comprehensive assessment of iron concentration, encompassing 0, 0.4, 20, 40, 80 and 160 μM, to evaluate their effects on nodulation (Extended Data Fig. 1g–n). The number of infection threads, nodule primordia, nodules and nitrogenase activity all increased up to and peaked at 40 μM but dramatically decreased at 80 μM Fe (Fig. 1a–g). Nodules barely formed at 160 μM Fe, although a few infection threads and primordia were observed (Fig. 1a–g).

manual_retrieved_paragraphs.text: Among the detected candidates, Glyma.05g237500 contains metal-ion-binding and DNA-binding domains and is predicted to be an E3 ubiquitin ligase, which isconservedinplants(ExtendedDataFig.3a).ItsArabidopsis orthologue BRUTUS (AtBTS) is an iron sensor that negatively regulates responses to iron deficiency. We therefore assigned Glyma.05g237500 as BTSa on the basis of its phylogenetic relationship with AtBTS (Extended Data Fig. 3a). This led us to wonder whether BTSa potentially integrates iron and nodulation cues in soybean. To test this, we first validated the NSP1a–BTSa interaction. Full-length BTSa can interact with NSP1a in a yeast two-hybrid assay (Fig. 3a). This interaction occurs in planta in the nucleus and BTSa3×HA could be co-immunoprecipitated with NSP1a–GFP (Fig. 3b,c), thus confirming that BTSa is indeed an NSP1a-interacting partner. To dissect which domain(s) mediate(s) the interaction of BTSa with NSP1a, we split BTSa into an N-terminal fragment (BTSa-NTer) that includes its three haemerythrin (HHE) cation-binding domains, and a C-terminal fragment (BTSa-CTer) containing a CHY-type zinc-finger domain, a Rubredoxin-type fold and RING zinc-finger domain (Fig. 3d). In yeast, BTSa-CTer, but not BTSa-NTer, could interact with NSP1a (Fig. 3a), indicating the CHY-type/ RING zinc-finger-containing domains are sufficient for this interaction.

manual_retrieved_paragraphs.text: We next generated two independent btsa btsb double-knockout mutants (assigned btsa btsb-1 and btsa btsb-2) by clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats–CRISPR associated 9 (CRISPR–Cas9) and evaluated their nodulation performance. Both mutant alleles have premature stop codons, express truncated BTSa and BTSb proteins containing partial HHE domains, and show no evidence of off-target edits to the corresponding target sites for BTSc and BTSd (Extended Data Fig. 4e–g). The number of infection threads, nodule primordia and nodules in both btsa btsb double mutants was markedly lower than in wild-type (WT) Wm82 controls (Fig. 3i–n), suggesting a positive role in soybean nodulation. Consistent with the impaired-nodulation phenotypes, NIN1a induction by rhizobia in the wild type was strongly attenuated in the btsa btsb-1 mutant (Fig. 3o). Taken together, these data suggest that BTSa and BTSb are required for nodulation by enhancing pro-nodulation signalling activity. To investigate whether BTSa and BTSb have distinct roles in nodulation, we expressed BTSa or BTSb under the control of the ubiquitin promoter or their native promoter in the btsa btsb mutant. The expression of BTSa or BTSb in the btsa btsb mutant completely restored its nodulation phenotype (Extended Data Fig. 5a–c). In addition, we generated single btsa and btsb mutants, and nodule numbers and nitrogenase activity were comparable to those in the wild type (Extended Data Fig. 5d–k). These results indicate that BTSa and BTSb have similar roles in regulating nodulation.

To confirm the monoubiquitination sites, we mutated all three lysine residues in Nter (NSP1aN3KR), both lysine residues in Cter (NSP1aC2KR) or all five lysine residues (NSP1a5KR), and tested their ubiquitination activity in vivo. manual_retrieved_paragraphs.text: Here we show that iron is a key driver of nodulation because symbiotic nodules cannot form without iron, even under conditions of sufficient light and low nitrogen. We further identify an iron optimum for soybean nodulation and the iron sensor BRUTUS A (BTSa) which acts as a hub for integrating iron and nodulation cues. BTSa is induced by rhizobia, binds to and is stabilized by iron. In turn, BTSa stabilizes and enhances the transcriptional activation activity of pro-nodulation transcription factor NSP1a by monoubiquitination from its RING domain and consequently activates nodulation signalling. Monoubiquitination of NSP1 by BTS is conserved in legumes to trigger nodulation under iron sufficiency. Thus, iron status is an essential cue to trigger nodulation and BTSa integrates cues from rhizobial infection and iron status to orchestrate host responses towards establishing symbiotic nitrogen fixation.
